entry.title: Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Legend and Beloved Shakespearean Actor, Dead at 86
entry.summary: Patrick Stewart, the Emmy and Tony-winning 'Star Trek' actor, is dead at 86.
entry.content:
Sir Patrick Stewart, the beloved stage and screen star known for his role as Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” has died at the age of 86 years old. News of his death was first reported by The New York Times.

More to come…

entry.title: Curry Barker Drops Surprise New Short Film ‘Mama Bear’ — Watch
entry.summary: The five-minute film, which Barker wrote, directed, and edited, was released on his That's a Bad Idea YouTube channel.
entry.content:
We still have to wait until May 2027 for Curry Barker‘s “Anything But Ghosts” to hit theaters, but fans of the “Obsession” writer/director have a new project to tide them over.

Barker has written, directed, and edited a new short film titled “Mama Bear,” which was released on his That’s a Bad Idea YouTube channel on Thursday morning. The five-minute project, which was sponsored by Microsoft, stars Jon Lee Richardson as Floyd, a young man whose nap is interrupted by some very disturbing phone calls that quickly change the course of his day. Katie Sarife, Ericka Kreuz, and Joshua Snyder co-star. Check out the film below.

Barker continues to enjoy one of the biggest breakout years we’ve seen from a filmmaker in recent memory. After “Obsession” was acquired by Focus Features at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival, it went on to gross over $500 million at the global box office this spring. Barker quickly became one of Hollywood’s most in-demand filmmakers, lining up a slate of projects that includes a “Texas Chainsaw Massacre” reboot for A24 and a mysterious original horror movie that landed him an eight-figure deal from Universal. And Barker had already completed “Anything But Ghosts,” a supernatural comedy that sees him co-star with his longtime filmmaking partner Cooper Tomlinson, before “Obsession” even opened.

Related Stories
The Netflix Original Movie Experiment Has Failed — and Netflix Will Be All the Better for It
Rare Stanley Kubrick Interview Headed to TCM’s ‘Plot Thickens’ Podcast as Bonus Episode

It led to Barker receiving IndieWire’s inaugural Future of Filmmaking Award at our recent Los Angeles summit. During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at the event, Barker spoke about his roots making independent short films and how it helped him refine his voice ahead of “Obsession.”

“I definitely learned from the comment section quite a bit,” Barker said of his experiencing posting his shorts on the That’s a Bad Idea channel. “I think the main thing I would take away is how smart the audience is. I think if I hadn’t learned that early on, I might write my dialogue differently. Maybe I’d write more exposition, maybe I’d not feel so confident that people were understanding me. That was invaluable, to see ‘Oh my god, this little thing, they are picking up on it! They are understanding these nuances.’”

entry.title: The Netflix Original Movie Experiment Has Failed — and Netflix Will Be All the Better for It
entry.summary: Netflix spent the last 10 years trying to render movie theaters obsolete. Now the company is giving up just in time to avoid becoming obsolete itself.
entry.content:
In April 2025, somehow only 18 months ago, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos participated in a public conversation that began with Time magazine’s editor-in-chief asking him a simple question: “Have you destroyed Hollywood?” It was meant as a cheeky icebreaker, and Sarandos — a smirk cracking across his face — gave the exact response you would expect from a disruptor of his wealth and power: “No, we’re saving Hollywood.”

They were saving Hollywood from the very reason it exists in the first place, and the reason — the only reason — why it continues to exert a peerlessly disproportionate influence on the collective imagination: movie theaters. “We’re in a period of transition,” Sarandos elaborated later in the panel. “Folks grew up thinking, ‘I want to make movies on a gigantic screen and have strangers watch them [and to have them] play in the theater for two months and people cry and sold-out shows’ …It’s an outdated concept.”

Related Stories
Rare Stanley Kubrick Interview Headed to TCM’s ‘Plot Thickens’ Podcast as Bonus Episode
AMC Releases ‘Dune 3’ Two-Headed Sandworm Popcorn Bucket That Manages to Look Even More NSFW

Cut to: October 2026. Hollywood is in a more precarious state than ever, and Netflix just rented out New York’s biggest AMC to stage a trailer premiere for the most crucial movie the company has ever made, an event where “Narnia” director Greta Gerwig was interviewed by Stephen Colbert in front of a massive IMAX screen as an audience of journalists munched on candy and popcorn. The screen was gigantic. Gerwig cried. When “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” opens in theaters next February, it will play there exclusively for (almost) two months before it’s available to watch on Netflix. Sarandos was right about one thing: We are in a period of transition. It’s just not the transition he had in mind.

Ever since Netflix entered the straight-to-streaming film space with “Beasts of No Nation” back in 2015, their ultimate goal — as unstated as it is unambiguous — has been nothing less than the complete elimination of movie theaters. They became the first content delivery service to transform into a major Hollywood studio, and then the first major Hollywood studio to try to transform Hollywood into a content delivery service. For more than 100 years, the film industry depended on selling movie tickets; Netflix’s agenda was to cut out the middleman and make subscribing to the service feel as obligatory as owning a smartphone. They even bought a few historic theaters along the way to make the process as smooth and gentle as possible.

Netflix didn’t operate that way because they’re more evil than any of the other movie studios (not even Sarandos has the hubris required to compete with Davids Zaslav and Ellison in that regard) — they operated that way because they’re a tech company that only became a movie studio as a means to an end. And tech companies have a funny way of acting like fourth-dimensional colonizers whenever they get too close to the arts.

If your business is to make things that people want to see, your top priority is to produce movies — ideally but infrequently good movies — and project them in large auditoriums where customers can pay a modest fee to experience them as they were meant to be seen. If your business is to sell people on a future they may not want to see, your top priority is to make the present seem obsolete. The present can become the past in a second, but it takes billions of dollars to make that process feel slower than it should. To make the present feel worthless and unwanted before its time is up. To convince people that it isn’t just passing by, but also holding them back.

Sarandos might be a lifelong cinephile whom Netflix originally hired for his deep background in film distribution, but there’s no doubt he’s a tech bro now. I can’t really blame him for that. The guy is both a product and an emblem of his times, and though I’m hard-pressed to think of another studio executive who’s ever made my blood run hotter on such a regular basis, I suspect that the likes of Darryl F. Zanuck and Louis B. Mayer would’ve spouted all the same bullshit had they been tasked with measuring “view hours” and competing against Mr. Beast for our attention. That’s just how tech bros have to talk. Their business models, stock prices, and corporate mystiques require them to act like weird ambassadors from the world of tomorrow — smiling and casual but always bent on destroying whatever it takes to bring their vision of the future to bear.

This is why Netflix has played by Hollywood’s rules only as much as it had to, even when sticking to its prime directive meant leaving free money on the table. They put “movies” into “theaters” to qualify them for awards and keep talent from setting the company’s server farms on fire. But even when major directors pleaded for longer windows — and even when there was a clear public demand for the same thing, as was famously the case with “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery” in 2022 — the millions Netflix might have earned in movie ticket sales were no match for the billions they stood to gain from rendering the concept of movie tickets obsolete.

Some filmmakers got the bag, delivered their content, and escaped with their dignity intact. Others happily gulped down the Kool-Aid and embraced a subscription-driven future where satisfying audiences was no longer part of the equation. As Joe Russo put it while promoting “The Gray Man,” everyone’s favorite and most well-remembered film of 2022: “This idea that the theater is a sacred space is bullshit.” Fair enough — if I knew I was about to direct “The Electric State,” I probably wouldn’t be able to shut up about how awful it is that people have to watch movies in public, where the expectation is they’ll sit through the entire thing and maybe even enjoy themselves. It’s barbaric.

Russo also went on to decry the “elitism” of the theatrical experience, echoing — or anticipating — Sarandos’ argument that many people across the country can’t easily get to a multiplex anymore. We’re all trying to find the guy who did that, but the point stands. I will never forget that Ava DuVernay, an outspoken advocate of Netflix’s agenda from the beginning, could only screen “A Wrinkle in Time” in her theater-less hometown of Compton because she convinced Disney to build a pop-up cinema inside a local community center. Ask Netflix to address the lack/uneven distribution of movie theaters, and their solution would be to put them all out of business (all of the ones they don’t own, anyway).

Netflix’s throw-out-the-baby-with-the-bathwater approach hinged on the presumption that people would happily forfeit the possibility of enjoying a proper theatrical experience in exchange for the promise of being able to enjoy “Bright” at home. Like all such acts of mass enshittification, that pivot was sold to the public as progress — as part of a devil’s bargain that sacrificed creativity at the altar of convenience. And, like all such acts of mass enshittification, it was made possible by the fact that the system it was meant to supplant had grown complacent. It’s hard to defend the Union Square Regal as a holy temple of the arts when 10 of its screens are playing Guy Ritchie’s live-action remake of “Aladdin” or whatever.

Of course, that was a blockbuster from the before times, and the COVID pandemic only further empowered Netflix to fulfill its mission. Not only were multiplexes shuttered for months (or years) on end, but the legacy studios fell over themselves to help their streaming rivals make semi-permanent inroads with the public. If parties had been safe to host in December 2020, Netflix would surely have thrown a generational rager to celebrate Warner Bros.’ decision to release “Dune,” “The Suicide Squad,” and 15 other major titles directly to HBO Max. Even as the pandemic began to subside and “Top Gun: Maverick” took flight at the box office two summers later, it seemed as if movie theaters — and the culture that sustained them — would never truly recover from such an unprecedented self-devaluation of corporate assets.

But then a funny thing happened: People kept going to the movies. In fits and starts at first, and then more regularly. In 2023, monocultural events like “Barbenheimer” had to be hyped and telegraphed months in advance before they reached critical mass. By the fall of 2026, a three-hour documentary about a blonde fraudster could become a nationally sold-out sensation with less than five weeks of lead time (although Elizabeth Holmes would argue, of course, that it always could have done that). Altogether, this year’s domestic box office is on track to reach $10 billion, almost matching the numbers from 2019.

There are a number of reasons for that, but I think this is the biggest one: As soon as screens reopened, the movies as a medium were immediately redefined by the ability to experience them in theaters. In an article published almost 10 years ago on this very website, I asked, “When you watch something on Netflix, are you watching a movie, or are you having a movie-like experience?” It was a question prompted by the dawning realization that “film” was becoming something of a misnomer in a world where content was classified less by the nature of its production than by the mechanism of its distribution — and by the gnawing sense that movies weren’t really being seen on Netflix, even on the off chance that someone was actually able to find a good one to watch on the service.

Since then, Netflix has doubled and quadrupled down on the bet that people wouldn’t sweat the difference between algorithmic streaming content and traditional studio fare. Between movies that had been made to satisfy a data point, and movies that had benefited from — or at least been put through — a more elaborate development process. The company hasn’t been completely immune to producing good films, and they’ve certainly spent a lot of money to acquire a variety of great ones (for every “Emilia Pérez” there’s at least one “May December” and several must-see documentaries), but unadvertised vanity runs did little to distinguish masterpieces like “Power of the Dog” from starry imitation slop like “The Adam Project,” and lower-profile gems like “They Cloned Tyrone” and “The World Is Yours” were practically guaranteed to be lost in the shuffle.

Meanwhile, the more determined Netflix became to mimic Hollywood entertainment at home, the further they widened the self-evident perception gap between DTV junk and IMAX-worthy spectacle. “Red Notice” may have been “viewed” by every person on Earth, but nobody remembers watching it. The difference between that and a similarly putrid theatrical release with one of the same stars (let’s go with “Black Adam”) is the difference between scrolling across a funny meme on your phone (face blank and eyes dead as you retweet it with the caption “lol stop I’m fucking DECEASED”) and enjoying a lived experience that has the chance to be remembered by virtue of its shared and unimpeachable reality. To quote Jia Tolentino’s “Trick Mirror,” the more difficult the 21st century makes it to “differentiate between the pretext for an experience, the record of that experience, and the experience itself,” the deeper that movie theaters will become reingrained as a determinative element of the movies themselves. The more difficult AI makes it to differentiate between slop and spectacle, the more people will unconsciously privilege the legitimacy a proper release confers, even on the biggest pieces of shit.

They call it “effort-signaling,” the way labor becomes “an integral character to the point where the final product ends up being a secondary concern.” And by “they,” I, of course, mean “a tweet that I saw while I was writing this article.” Releasing a movie — even a bad movie — requires effort. The future that Ted Sarandos has brought to us (and us to) with the inflexible weight of a destiny is, to his great consternation, a future where people will only be willing to invest themselves in things that someone else has credibly invested themselves in first.

It’s no wonder that Netflix’s streaming competitors have suffered from similar woes in this space. “F1” and “Killers of the Flower Moon” did major numbers at home on the backs of robust theatrical rollouts, while most movies that went straight to Apple TV barely seem to exist. Remember the Justin Timberlake vehicle “Palmer”? Apparently I wrote like 1,200 words about it. What about “Wolfs,” the George Clooney/Brad Pitt/Austin Abrams action-comedy that pivoted away from a wide release less than six weeks before it came out, immediately became Apple TV’s most-viewed film ever, and then sank into the bottomless abyss of lost media just as fast? Not lost, I suppose, but hiding in plain sight.

It’s likewise no wonder that the one Netflix movie that blossomed into a bona fide sensation, of the roughly 4,000 original films they’ve released since 2015, was 1.) produced outside the company, 2.) clearly excellent, and 3.) squarely targeted at children who could obsess over it with their friends all summer long and inhabit its characters through dress-up and singing. “K-Pop Demon Hunters” was a perfect vessel for the kind of engagement Netflix’s entire business model exists to diminish, and I suspect its success was a wake-up call — or at least an early warning sign — that Netflix desperately needed to be saved from itself.

To the company’s sincere credit, they’ve recently made strides towards that end. Netflix’s org chart might be in crisis, and its subscribers are growing increasingly restless about the awful cadence of content worth caring about. But the inevitable pivot toward real theatrical releases will meaningfully raise the profile of their exclusive film titles in the coming months, even if few of them perform as well as “La Bola Negra” has so far.

That pivot represents a rare about-face for a tech giant that has sought to remake the world in its own image, consumer happiness be damned. In the same interview where Sarandos called movie theaters an outdated concept, he also insisted that “Netflix is a very consumer-focused company,” and that “we really do care that we deliver the program to you in a way you want to watch it.” At long last, they seem to have figured out which way that might be.

entry.title: ‘Nocturne’ Review: Stephen Graham and Bill Camp Brighten Up Apple’s Staid Crime Thriller for Sad Dads
entry.summary: A solid cast can't quite make 'Nocturne' more than the sum of its very familiar parts: serial killer, retired cop, revenge, secrets, DelCo accents.
entry.content:
Three scenes in “Nocturne” nearly knocked me out of my chair: two from excitement, one from exasperation. For a bit of fun, read on and guess which scene inspired which reaction. Or I hope it’s fun, at least, because the dour “Nocturne” is only fun for die-hard fans of the genre — and its cast.

The first stand-out scene will arrive at a different time for every viewer, but for me, it’s shortly after onscreen text identifies the setting as “Fairhaven, Pennsylvania.” That’s when the buzzer goes off, the one that formed in critics’ minds after “Mare of Easttown” and “Task” helped popularize the sound of Delaware County. Now, any show set in the Keystone State — especially a crime show — starts on high alert for lowly accents. And “Nocturne” does not disappoint.

Related Stories
Hoorae’s Microdramas Found 580 Million Views. Can TikTok Get Hollywood Working Again? — Watch
‘The Gilded Age’ Cast on Returning for Season 4 After a Ratings Surge: ‘It’s Go Big or Go Home’

“What are yoo doing here?” Jonah (Liev Schreiber) asks his surrogate daughter, Saga (Zazie Beetz), when she shows up to tell the retired cop that his last case — the case that “broke him” (Beetz doesn’t use an accent, so she says her O’s sans inflection) — is active again. One of two missing kids has been found. The clock is ticking to find the other. The cops already called in the feds (specifically, Poorna Jagannathan’s zero-fucks special agent in charge), but they don’t know what Jonah does! “I know yoo suffered, and yoor life was ohver,” Ida (Chrissy Metz) tells Jonah, begging him to look for her missing kids one… last… time.

So he does! Of course he does. The man is living in a cabin with a giant murder board on the wall, hiking the woods with the faintest hope he’ll stumble across the siblings he was assigned to find oh so many years ago. If that’s not enough evidence that Jonah is haunted, he’s also building a treehouse for his own absent family, who Saga says won’t be back. What happened to them, and why Jonah remains obsessed with this one unsolved case, are details that get slowly dripped out, like in every other sad-dad detective show that stretches a movie-length premise over 10 hourlong episodes.

But hearing that sweet murder-durder voice spring ferth from Ray Donovan is, quite frankly, werth the price of admission for those of us holding an outsized appreciation for actors attempting difficult regional dialects. To be honest, there could be more. Beetz, despite her character growing up in the area, uses her regular voice, perhaps because Saga is an undercover FBI agent who needs to live with a less telling, more neutral intonation. Or perhaps because Beetz is already unconvincing as an undercover FBI agent, introduced via a poorly staged drug bust that hangs the actor out to dry, long before she struggles to match Stephen Graham‘s serial-killer freak.

Ah yes, there’s a serial killer. The missing kids tie back to Jurek Walter, played by the “Adolescence” Emmy winner with an accent. In the rare instances he speaks, that’s quite fun: a quiet mix of carefully considered words metered out in whispered spurts and soft, equally sporadic vowel sounds. As the Hannibal Lecter type — a brilliant, terrifying killer whose positioning behind bars does little to dissuade our detectives from believing he’s still actively offing people out in the world — Graham doesn’t overdo it. His archvillain, who likes to bury people alive almost as much as he likes psychologically manipulating folks into self-harm, channels his sinister vibes with steady stares imbued with confidence. He likes to show off how much he knows about strangers through observation alone, and then uses those same skills to lure them into his devious plans.

But I digress. “Nocturne” does little to distinguish itself from the oft-copied “Silence of the Lambs” dynamic. Jonah and Jurek share only a handful of brief scenes together through the seven episodes screened for critics, and their moments together feel less electric than perfunctory. Co-showrunners John Hlavin and Rowan Joffé give their actors room to play, but within the bounds of a faux-prestige crime thriller (based on the Swedish novel “The Sandman” by Lars Kepler). Vivid locations (go birds), a solemn tone (so dark, so serious), and a talented cast are as capital-B Big as “Nocturne” gets.

At least, so far: The last episode screened for critics finally puts a few clarifying cards on the table, and those major reveals are both clichéd and annoying. I shan’t spoil them here, but how “Nocturne’s” mystery starts to resolve itself betrays the creeping, detailed investigation that makes up a bulk of the story by settling for the easiest and most obvious explanations possible. Astute viewers will likely spot warning signs much sooner, when characters make unearned assumptions to move things along, or when all-too-convenient mistakes occur to string out necessary questions for another few hours.

“Nocturne” relies on its premium-streaming trappings to gloss over these glitches, and depending on your love for the dirty crime drama they’re polishing, they may be an acceptable price to pay for such pleasures as my third-and-final dumbfounding delight: Bill Camp, who plays Fairhaven police chief Dave Ellison, and Ken Leung, as some FBI big-wig, in the same scene! Together! Camp and Leung! The dynamic duo you didn’t know you needed! Better still, there’s reason to believe they’ll share multiple scenes together, as Leung doesn’t appear until the seventh episode, and Camp is in the whole damn show!

Herein lies the not-so-secret sauce behind well-cast genre fare (shout-out to casting director Avy Kaufman): If you hire invested, eminently watchable actors, they can make tired tropes sing. Sure, it’s far more exciting to see Leung sink his teeth into a layered, complex, and specific role like he has on “Industry,” but in a few short seconds here, as the big-city suit trying to flex on a small-town cop, he can still snap you back to attention.

Your drifting focus picks up on a sly note of sarcasm when he questions the locals’ unique methodology. Your drooping eyes fixate on his calculated gaze as it darts around the office before landing, again and again, on the supposed colleague he’s blatantly interrogating. His physical presence, aided subtly by his refined houndstooth overcoat and matching gray buzzcut, clashes with the unkempt cop before him — which, it must be said, only makes it funnier when Camp presents his bulging black eye, shaggy crop of hair, and stubbly, unamused face directly to Leung’s sharp, clean, superior officer, as if to say, “Do you really think your fancy clothes and bossy attitude can intimidate me?” And Leung wordlessly responds, “I don’t care.”

The scene is a classic jurisdictional dispute, plain and simple. But Camp and Leung bring just enough personal vehemence and lived-in decision-making to make this clash more memorable than 99 percent of the 99 million that preceded it. That’s why you hire them. That’s why you hire the actor Richard Price hired to root Stephen King’s mystical boogeyman story in an irrefutable reality in “The Outsider.” That’s why you hire the actor Chris Mundy and Damon Lindelof hired to ground the shape-shifting alien mystery in “Lanterns.” That’s why you hire the actor Jonathan Demme hired to help legitimize the crazy mind-control plot in “The Manchurian Candidate.” (OK, I guess Denzel helped a bit, too.)

As The New York Times’ chief TV critic James Poniewozick likes to say, you can’t turn a bad show into a good show simply by hiring good actors. “Nocturne” proves that as much as any single show can. But for anyone in the tank for a grim cop vs. killer story, it’s just a little bit better than it should be thanks to the people in front of the camera. These folks know how to get a scene on its feet — and how to make an audience follow suit.

Grade: C

“Nocturne” premieres Friday, October 30 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 10) on December 25.

entry.title: ‘Wicker’ Is Even Better — and Hornier — in 4DX
entry.summary: Black Bear's one-night-only presentation of their Sundance hit 'Wicker' in 4DX reveals new possibilities for the format.
entry.content:
Ever since 4DX technology debuted in 2009 for Seoul screenings of James Cameron’s “Avatar,” the immersive format has been associated primarily with spectacles and franchise films; if you’ve been to a 4DX auditorium, you probably went to see a Marvel movie or a “Fast and Furious” sequel. The idea seems to be that 4DX — a presentation system that “enhances” movies with physical effects like shaking seats, wind, flashing lights, snow, water, and scents — is best utilized in action films where the onscreen chaos is intensified by the chaos of being yanked around in your chair while nozzles spray air and water in your face.

For years, I avoided 4DX like the plague after an ill-advised trip to see “Maleficent: Mistress of Evil.” When motion sickness set in before the end of the first reel, I figured I had experienced enough 4DX to last me for the rest of my life. Then last year, while writing a piece comparing six release formats for “One Battle After Another,” I gave 4DX another shot and was surprised by how much I enjoyed it. Seeing Paul Thomas Anderson’s masterpiece with effects that included air blasting in my ear to simulate gunshots and the seat rocking to simulate Sean Penn’s masturbation added an unexpected dimension to the viewing experience.

Related Stories
Yes, That’s a Wicker Penis: Inside Alexander Skarsgård’s Wild ‘Wicker’ Transformation
Will ‘Wicker’ Be Black Bear’s First Big Breakout?

Since then, I’ve caught a couple more movies in 4DX, from an epic that typically uses the format (“The Odyssey”) to a contained thriller that barely uses it at all (“Verity”). Then, last night, I caught the “Citizen Kane” of 4DX movies, the one that uses the format the way it should have always been implemented — not as a form of cinematic shock treatment designed to amplify onscreen violence, but as an expression of sensual pleasure. I give you, ladies and gentlemen, “Wicker” in 4DX.

Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson’s offbeat love story between a fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) and a man made of wicker (Alexander Skarsgård) has been a hot topic among cinephiles since its audience-pleasing debut at Sundance earlier this year. Hilarious but also genuinely romantic and poignant, it’s a true original. It’s also, as viewers could tell even from the trailer, fearlessly sexy, with several scenes of woman-on-wicker lovemaking that end with Colman’s bed demolished.

As soon as audiences started discovering the movie, the joke began making its way around Film Twitter and Letterboxd: where was the 4DX version of “Wicker?” Distributor Black Bear heard the joke and decided to make it a reality, scheduling one-night-only 4DX screenings at around 60 U.S. screens last night. If Southern California is any indication, the screenings were a wild success; the one I attended at a local Regal was nearly sold out, as were all the engagements within a 30-mile radius of Los Angeles.

And the 4DX presentation of “Wicker” did not disappoint. While many of the effects were typical of 4DX — the seat moving in unison with different characters, water hitting your face in rainy scenes — it didn’t take long for “Wicker” to demonstrate that it would be a more inventive, more adult exploitation of the format. The first sign of the picture’s flair for 4DX innovation came when Colman peed into her chamber pot and then tossed the contents out the door — and into the audience’s face, as we were all doused with water representing Colman’s urine.

Similarly cheeky gags occurred throughout the presentation, but the moment we were all waiting for was Colman and Skarsgård’s wedding night. The scene did not disappoint; as the fisherwoman and her wicker husband threw each other around the bed in ecstasy, the 4DX chairs tossed the audience in perfectly timed thrusts, creating a communal experience unlike any I’ve ever had in a movie theater. To be blunt, it felt like 150 strangers were all simulating sex with each other, and the, for lack of a better word, release at the end was exhilarating. We all erupted with applause when the bed split apart, and our shared ecstasy had reached its climax.

It makes one wonder: Is the true future of 4DX softcore pornography? There’s nothing really special about being jerked side to side while Superman flies through Metropolis, but feeling like you’re humping Olivia Colman (or being humped by Alexander Skarsgård) really brings people together. The possibilities for expanding the format’s potential are endless. Just as movies like “Titanic” and “Terminator 2” are retrofitted with 3D for special re-releases, 4DX could bring back “9 1/2 Weeks” and “Basic Instinct” in all their steamy, thrusting glory.

The fact that this was only a one-night event made it feel undeniably special, but today Black Bear announced that additional 4DX screenings are now scheduled throughout the next week. I’m glad the experiment was a success and has inspired an extension — the pleasures of “Wicker” in 4DX should not be limited to a select few.

Visit the “Wicker” website for information on additional 4DX screenings.

entry.title: Rare Stanley Kubrick Interview Headed to TCM’s ‘Plot Thickens’ Podcast as Bonus Episode
entry.summary: TCM host Ben Mankiewicz will share Stanley Kubrick's 1972 interview with Newsday film critic Joseph Gelmis on January 7, 2027, on the podcast.
entry.content:
We’re always talking about Stanley Kubrick around these parts. But lately, the “Shining” and “2001: A Space Odyssey” director is even more present in the cinephile conversation thanks to Criterion’s just-released, staggering box set covering Kubrick’s entire filmography. (Including the much-debated, rare international cut of “The Shining.”)

But also currently airing on podcast platforms is a new season of TCM host Ben Mankiewicz‘s “The Plot Thickens,” an entire slate of episodes dedicated solely to the master filmmaker, who died in 1999 just before “Eyes Wide Shut” was released. IndieWire has some new exclusive news about the podcast: Two bonus episodes will be added to the already 11-episode run.

Related Stories
AMC Releases ‘Dune 3’ Two-Headed Sandworm Popcorn Bucket That Manages to Look Even More NSFW
‘Everytime’ Trailer: The Mind-Bending Grief Portrait That’s Left Audiences Spellbound Since Cannes

Turner Classic Movies has shared that it will release Stanley Kubrick’s rare, complete 1972 interview with Newsday film critic Joseph Gelmis as a bonus episode of “The Plot Thickens.” Available January 7, 2027, the episode presents the full conversation. So far, it’s only been excerpted across the season.

This “Clockwork Orange”-era interview “captures the famously private Kubrick in an expansive conversation with Gelmis, discussing his approach to directing actors and his beginnings as an independent filmmaker alongside personal interests, including football and his beloved pets,” per TCM.

In the episode, Kubrick also opines about a perennial cinephile topic: how home viewing might reshape moviegoing, even while advocating for the theatrical experience. While discussing “A Clockwork Orange,” Kubrick also recounts wearing a copper bracelet he believed relieved shoulder pain from playing ping-pong.

“Kubrick had a reputation for being private, but here you get to spend nearly three hours listening to him talk about his work and his everyday life,” said Ben Mankiewicz. “There’s pleasure in letting the conversation unfold; hearing what he takes seriously, what exasperates him, and what amuses him. What film lover isn’t curious about how Stanley Kubrick sees the world?”

Created in partnership with Criterion, the new “The Plot Thickens” season, “Stanley,” explores Kubrick’s life and career through archival audio and interviews with those who knew him and worked with him, with new episodes every Thursday.

TCM will also release a recording of its sold-out Kubrick panel presented in partnership with American Cinematheque at the Aero Theatre as an additional bonus episode on January 14, 2027. Moderated by Mankiewicz, the discussion features filmmaker Jason Reitman, dialect coach Elizabeth Himelstein, and former L.A. Times critic Kenneth Turan. The panel was held before a screening of “Dr. Strangelove.”

Both bonus episodes will be available on all major podcast apps and platforms, including Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube. Listen to our ”Screen Talk” podcast episode with Ben Mankiewicz, where he, along with co-hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio, ranks Kubrick’s top five films, here.

entry.title: AMC Releases ‘Dune 3’ Two-Headed Sandworm Popcorn Bucket That Manages to Look Even More NSFW
entry.summary: AMC has release two 'Dune 3' sandworm buckets, including one with two heads.
entry.content:
It’s double trouble.

AMC Theatres has released the first look at its new “Dune: Part Three” collectible popcorn buckets. And to send Paul Atreides off in style, the theatre chain has not one, but two designs, including one bucket that has two sandworm heads. The other, a “Sandworm Thumper” bucket, boasts a “working Thumper design.” For those not versed in all things spice, the Thumpers are what Fremen warriors place in the desert sands to summon the worms from their subterranean homes.

The designs are, how shall we put it, a little NSFW. Their resemblance to popular sex toys was parodied in a SNL sketch in which a frisky adolescent’s thoughts turned to something other than popcorn when he looked at the sandworm’s gaping mouth.

Related Stories
‘Everytime’ Trailer: The Mind-Bending Grief Portrait That’s Left Audiences Spellbound Since Cannes
Reality Check: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Faces a Long Road to the Oscars

The company said that the double sandworm bucket is perfect for couples, because it’s “easier to share popcorn.” There’s also a light-up cup, though no word on pricing. Buckets typically cost in the neighborhood of $25. “Dune: Part Three” opens December 18, 2026, and brings back franchise stars Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, and Rebecca Ferguson, as well as director Denis Villeneuve.

The collectibles have become big business for the chain, with AMC chief Adam Aron projecting the company will make more than $100 million selling the themed buckets this year.

AMC has released collectible buckets timed to major films such as “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but the chain acknowledged that all eyes were on them for their “Dune” follow-up.

“The AMC Sandworm popcorn bucket for ‘Dune: Part Two’ became a viral phenomenon, and we knew that ‘Dune’ fans would have high expectations for what came next,” said Hank Green, AMC’s senior VP of food and beverage. “From the moment we started planning the ‘Dune: Part Three’ collectibles, our goal was to exceed those fan expectations. The Sandworm Thumper and Double Sandworm collectibles take the experience to the next level with designs straight from the movie.”

In other words, cue the memes.

entry.title: ‘Everytime’ Trailer: The Mind-Bending Grief Portrait That’s Left Audiences Spellbound Since Cannes
entry.summary: Watch the first U.S. teaser for Sandra Wollner's Cannes-winning 'Everytime,' opening in February 2027 after a November qualifying run.
entry.content:
Anyone who saw Sandra Wollner’s perversely creepy previous film, “The Trouble with Being Born,” might be left having no idea what to expect from her follow-up. That film was built around a child-sized android cast in resemblance to her master’s missing daughter — and it’s more than implied he’s sexually assaulting the girl, too.

Disturbing as it was, “The Trouble with Being Born” also announced Wollner’s aptitude for capturing grief from peculiar, underseen angles. And so her next movie, “Everytime,” while more generously empathetic, also takes on loss from a mind-bending perspective we’re not going to spoil. Since winning in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard, this German entry for the Best International Feature Film Oscar has bewitched festivalgoers from Toronto to New York. IndieWire shares the exclusive teaser below.

Related Stories
Reality Check: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Faces a Long Road to the Oscars
Barbara Barrie, Oscar-Nominated ‘Breaking Away’ and ‘Private Benjamin’ Star, Dies at 95

“Everytime” also just received Gotham Award nominations for Best International Feature, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay. Here, following a tragedy in Berlin, a mother, Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her youngest daughter, Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her older daughter’s former boyfriend, Lux (Tristán López), take what turns out to be a profound holiday to the Spanish island of Tenerife — one where the environment appears to convene and reshape itself around their shared, unimaginable loss.

“Everytime” will play for a one-week Oscar-qualifying run at New York City’s Lincoln Center starting November 6, with the full theatrical date following February 12, 2027. 1-2 Special distributes the film after purchasing “Everytime” out of Cannes. The New York-based distributor also has Marine Atlan’s Cannes-winning “La Gradiva,” entering theaters in December.

“Its ineffable power belongs to how matter-of-factly Wollner tears apart the fabric of her film’s reality at the same time as she threads it together,” Indiewire’s David Ehrlich wrote of “Everytime” in his Grade A review.

Watch the teaser for “Everytime” below.

entry.title: Reality Check: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Faces a Long Road to the Oscars
entry.summary: 'You Can See Everything' is a box office sensation. History and math tell us that probably won't lead to Oscars glory.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Everybody’s talking about the A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” and many Oscar prognosticators are jumping on board the Best Picture bandwagon. Don’t buy the hype.

While there’s a lot to admire about Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s entertaining nonfiction approach to parsing the distorted reality of disgraced Thanatos founder Elizabeth Holmes just before she went to prison, it’s still a long road for a surprise box-office documentary hit ($45 million domestic and counting) to garner enough Oscar votes for a Best Picture nomination.

Related Stories
Barbara Barrie, Oscar-Nominated ‘Breaking Away’ and ‘Private Benjamin’ Star, Dies at 95
A Flop at the Chinese Box Office Shows AI Still Has a Tough Road Ahead in Theaters

The folks who believe it’s possible are listening to the current buzz and noise, much of it from younger movie fans on social media, and the film‘s undeniable heat. A24’s brilliant “no spoilers” marketing campaign has pushed more moviegoers than usual into theaters early in the run. But the Academy membership is still senior-centric.

Here are the necessary steps for A24 to nab a BP nod.

Step One: Critic group wins. This week’s Gotham nomination for Best Documentary Feature is a start. The movie needs to land awards from the NYFCC, LAFCA, and NSFC. The Golden Globes will be no help, as they do not give a documentary prize. Critic support will add prestige and convince laggards to watch the movie on the Academy portal.

Step Two: Lure international voters. “YCSE” is an American movie, even if it confronts alternate reality issues familiar to everyone. It has yet to open overseas. Recognition from the European Film Awards or BAFTAs would show support outside North America. (Checking on eligibility)

Step Three: Legitimize the movie with the 750-member documentary branch, which is notorious for rejecting popular nonfiction like Morgan Neville’s “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?” and Brett Morgen’s “Jane.” Some doc voters harbor strong opinions about reenactments, which YCSE leans into in the second half. There’s a strong chance the doc branch will not nominate this movie.

Step Four: Figure Out Nathan Fielder. The offbeat, deliberately awkward creator behind TV series “The Rehearsal” and “The Curse” is an acquired taste. He’s been doing some press interviews and panels, but full-court glad-handing may not be his strong suit.

Step Five: Break out of the doc box. In the Oscars‘ 98-year history, no documentary has ever been nominated for Best Picture. Over the past two decades, none of the docs that have succeeded at the box office have made it, not even Michael Moore’s 2004 Palme d’Or winner “Fahrenheit 9/11” — which was ineligible for the Oscar because it played on TV before the contentious national election. Moore received two documentary Oscar nominations for “Sicko” and “Bowling for Columbine,” winning the prize for the latter.

Step Six: Beat out the A24 competition. Four movies are vying for Best Picture this year from A24. The distributor is also pushing Olivia Wilde’s four-hander “The Invite,” Jesse Eisenberg’s crowdpleaser “The Debut,” and rookie Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” (a more likely Original Screenplay nod). “No one has the bandwidth to do every film justice,” said one Oscar campaigner. “It’s hard for a studio to get more than two.”

Step Seven: Woo the actors. With more than 1,100 voters, the actors are the dominant branch in the Academy. On GoldDerby.com, Experts list Amanda Seyfried in the sixth spot as a Supporting Actor contender. (The movie is ranked eighth for Best Picture.) In “YCSE,” she performs transcripts as Elizabeth Holmes in various reenactments, whom she played in the TV series “The Dropout.” And she plays herself. This is a hard one to call. Many believe this is more about A24 hype than reality.

Step Eight: Do the Numbers. Look at branches of the Academy and count the ones that are likely to vote for this movie. The classic way of figuring out a Best Picture contender is to see where its support lies among the active 10,365 voters. That’s how I figured out that “F1” might make it to Best Picture last year. Some of the 750 documentary branch members will vote for “YCSE” and are the most likely to see the movie. Anyone can vote for Best Picture, but the doc is unlikely to win any craft nominations: animation (729), casting directors (191), cinematographers (326), costume designers (205), editors (421), hair & makeup (225), music (430), production design (446), production and technology (424, they don’t have a branch but they vote), short films (234), sound (575), and visual effects (679). More likely to vote for the movie are such non-crafts as artists representatives (266), directors (587), executives (770), marketing and public relations (672), producers (692), and writers (534). The movie has no script per se. But writers may appreciate its ingenious structure and evolution.

Finally, if “YCSE” were to become the first doc to score a Best Picture slot, it would likely do so without any other nominations.

entry.title: Barbara Barrie, Oscar-Nominated ‘Breaking Away’ and ‘Private Benjamin’ Star, Dies at 95
entry.summary: Barbara Barrie, the Oscar-nominated star of 'Breaking Away,' 'Barney Miller,' and 'Private Benjamin' had died at 95.
entry.content:
Barbara Barrie, a character actress best known for playing boisterous moms in “Breaking Away” and “Private Benjamin,” has died. She was 95.

Barrie’s daughter, Jane Harnick, told the New York Times that her mother had terminal cancer and said her death was “medically assisted.”

Barrie was an inveterate scene stealer who was a frequent presence on stage and screen. On Broadway, she appeared in the original cast of Stephen Sondheim’s “Company,” a revolutionary musical that examined relationships and commitment. Barrie earned a Tony Award nomination for her role in the 1970 production. Other Broadway credits included Neil Simon’s hit “California Suite.”

For her film work, Barrie won the best actress prize at the 1964 Cannes Film Festival for “One Potato, Two Potato,” an interracial romance, in which her character confronts prejudice while falling in love with a Black man. But it was “Breaking Away,” and her work as the blue-collar mother of a cycling enthusiast, that put Barrie on the map. She was nominated for best supporting sctress for the 1979 coming-of-age classic, then reprised the part in a 1980 TV series based on “Breaking Away,” earning an Emmy nomination.

Barrie also was known to audiences for her turn on the 1970s detective sitcom “Barney Miller,” portraying the wife of the title character. Other credits included the films “Judy Berlin,” “The Bell Jar,” and Disney’s “Hercules,” as well as appearances on “Law & Order” and “Suddenly Susan.”

Barrie was a published author. She wrote children’s books, as well as “Second Act” and “Don’t Die of Embarrassment,” which examined her battle with colorectal cancer.

entry.title: A Flop at the Chinese Box Office Shows AI Still Has a Tough Road Ahead in Theaters
entry.summary: A fully AI generated feature, 'Sanxingdui: Future Past,' flopped at the Chinese box office this past weekend, earning just $181,000.
entry.content:
One of the old adages of the film business was that people wouldn’t pay to watch an actor in theaters if they could see them for free on TV. Today, AI-generated content in China is ubiquitous, with a recent report suggesting that among the explosion of microdramas in China, nearly two-thirds of those videos are all generated by AI.

But it seems there’s a big difference between what audiences, even Chinese ones, will pay to buy a ticket for compared to what they will consume on their phones for free.

This past weekend, a fully, AI-generated feature film titled “Sanxingdui: Future Past” opened in Chinese theaters and grossed just RMB1.21 million, which is about $181,000, according to the film’s producer Bona Film Group. It’s the first AI feature to get the right to play on Chinese screens, and it makes it a big flop, as Bona in a recent blog post said the budget for the movie was 10 million yuan, which is about $1.5 million.

Related Stories
Hoorae’s Microdramas Found 580 Million Views. Can TikTok Get Hollywood Working Again? — Watch
What Do You Get When the ‘Texas Chainsaw’ Director Takes on the Marquis de Sade? The Kinky Pleasures of ‘Night Terrors’

That’s about the budget of a small indie, and perhaps more than you would’ve guessed when so much of the narrative around AI is that it’s going to cut costs and that you can make “Avatar” for next to nothing. But Bona says the film was produced over the course of two years from a team of 70 to 80 people, and some of the creators bristled at the idea that the images were created with a single click. In fact, the blog post says “Future Past” was being tweaked and technically still “shooting” up until a week before the film hit theaters.

Clearly, though, that level of artistry wasn’t evident on screen. An attendee told the international outlet AFP that the AI still “falls short” of a human-made, live-action production. “In the future, just like films, maybe decades later, it would get to a level when people are all willing to pay to watch,” she told AFP. “But for the moment, I think there would be very few who would.”

Bona had reason to believe that the film could attract a reasonable audience in theaters. “Sanxingdui: Future Past” originated as an AI microdrama series itself that managed nearly 200 million views. In fact, production has already begun on Bona’s second AI-generated feature, “Unplanned Operation in the Cold Moon,” and that the company has received requests to screen the movie in other countries outside of China.

The challenge though of releasing a 100-minute feature compared to a microdrama that could be just a few minutes in length is that it has to go through a content review process before it can be screened in theaters, so that speed to bring something new and fresh to market wasn’t there for “Sanxingdui.”

All of this will be something that the upcoming film from YouTuber and AI creator Gossip Goblin will be watching closely. His fully AI feature, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” is opening in U.S. theaters this December and is even launching international sales at the American Film Market next month. It’s the first such movie to receive a rating from the MPA, and it’s even intending to submit for eligibility at the Oscars for Best Animated Feature. Gossip Goblin has a large audience that he cultivates across numerous psychedelic, sprawling AI shorts, many of which belong to a connected story universe, so he’s hoping to emulate the Markiplier and “Iron Lung” playbook to draw a dedicated fanbase to theaters via a self-releasing strategy.

But whether it’s in China or America, people go to the theaters expecting a certain level of cinematic quality above what they can get at home on their phones. We’ll see if the “Sanxingdui” experiment ends up translating to American audiences.

entry.title: Hoorae’s Microdramas Found 580 Million Views. Can TikTok Get Hollywood Working Again? — Watch
entry.summary: Watch executives from Hoorae Media discuss their breakout hit 'Screen Time' and the future of microdramas at IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit.
entry.content:
The couples have secrets(!). The TV has been hijacked(!!). And somewhere between the next confession and its immediate cliffhanger(!!!), Issa Rae’s Hoorae Media is trying to figure out how to get Hollywood back to work. In “Screen Time,” the production company’s first microdrama, released on TikTok earlier this year, a double date becomes a waking nightmare when a sinister figure takes over one couple’s living room TV screen and demands the lovers come clean(?!)… or risk exposure.

For the people who made the juicy series, the stakes are less lurid but plenty urgent: Can a thriller told in minute-long segments sustain a business that keeps indie filmmakers, cast, and crew on set? So far, there’s reason to keep watching and, more encouragingly, to keep experimenting.

Related Stories
What Do You Get When the ‘Texas Chainsaw’ Director Takes on the Marquis de Sade? The Kinky Pleasures of ‘Night Terrors’
Slamdance Names Screenplay Competition Winners for 2026 — Read the Full List

By the time Hoorae executives Jax Clark and Dzifa Yador joined IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit on Saturday, October 17, “Screen Time” had accumulated nearly 580 million views across TikTok and its dedicated microdrama app, PineDrama.

“My favorite comment is, ‘Who put Netflix on my TikTok?’” Yador said. “It just really validated the fact that we did not abandon what it takes to build a premium product.” 580 million views is a lot of attention, by any standard. Whether that attention can sustain the people making microdramas is the question behind Hoorae’s developing business — and in a room full of eager film folks ready to roll up their sleeves, Clark and Yador made an appealingly practical case for finding out where bite-sized verticals can take their company and collaborators.

“How are we creating a sustainable pipeline that can bring new talent, new voices, new points of view into the industry?” Clark said. “As barriers to entry continue to get higher and the industry constricts and budgets are constrained, that’s continued to be an internal mission and engine for the company.”

Before bringing “Insecure” to HBO, Rae had already built an audience on YouTube with “The Mis-Adventures of Awkward Black Girl.” Hoorae’s microdrama effort returns to those digital roots through its TikTok distribution model, openly embraced brand partnerships, and a willingness to rethink what a day’s work — and even a story’s eventual audience — might look like.

“Obviously we work in television, we work in film, and now to be back in digital, which is where Issa really got her start and started building her audience has felt like a very beautiful full circle moment,” Clark said. (Notably, fellow summit speaker and inaugural Future of Filmmaking Award honoree Curry Barker knows something about that online runway: His reported $800 YouTube feature “Milk & Serial” preceded his theatrical breakout with “Obsession.”)

For Yador, the challenge was adapting Hoorae’s storytelling to the digital world’s existing habits.

“It wasn’t about trying to reimagine what storytelling is because we do that so well already,” she said. “Kudos to Jax and Issa and the entire team, but it was about how do we repackage it for the now, understanding where people are spending the most of their time on phones and how to continue to elevate the space so that it feels very much like a Hoorae product.”

Clark further described Hoorae’s ambitions as extending to creatives stuck in industry assistant jobs or “whatever writer purgatory they’re in,” with productions offering experience on set and in post. Anyone hoping to rescue an unproduced screenplay by rotating it 90 degrees should temper their expectations, she said. But if you’re willing to adapt to the microdrama world, there’s real opportunity.

“This isn’t a format where it’s like, ‘Hey, I have a feature script that no one invested in and now I’m just going to chop it up into minutes and we can make this a microdrama,’” Clark said. “It’s not an apples to apples conversion that happens. Part of it is talking to creatives who are willing to try something new and build something that maintains the integrity of the medium.”

Surely, though, anyone with a phone and a flair for betrayal could give it a shot, right? Maybe.

Yador said Hoorae spent two years studying vertical storytelling before diving into the space, and they don’t regret the prep. With “Screen Time,” Clark said, the central question was familiar to anyone who enjoys a good erotic thriller: “Can you really trust the person you go to sleep with every night?” But to make that hook work specifically for vertical, Hoorae assembled a team combining traditional filmmaking experience with unique expertise relevant excelling in the microdrama format.

“We have a blend of just talented filmmakers, but then we also have the top of the class in terms of people who have done verticals before,” Yador said. “We feel really confident working with actors who maybe haven’t done this before because we know we have the team to help educate them.

Amusingly, for cast members already accustomed to verticals, an assignment from Hoorae can actually mean dialing things down: “It’s actors who are maybe used to coming out on a hundred for every scene and we can tell them, actually we can ground this and we want you to try something new here and maybe play this more seriously and maybe riff a little bit,” Clark said.

Legibility is key, and even a carefully considered character arc has to survive the instability of a scrollable feed. After all, a viewer might meet these people in the finale and need to watch in reverse.

“Wherever you get dropped in has to feel just as propulsive and just as noteworthy as your pilot episode and sticky enough to keep you in there,” Yador explained. “And there’s kind of a machine in terms of the mechanics of how you develop a microdrama. And those are the engines that we’re talking about and they exist even in the finale.”

TikTok helps Hoorae navigate that unpredictability. Yador credited the platform with joining as a distribution partner as “Screen Time” production was wrapping, and with providing insights into what attracts viewers. The partnership, announced in April, provides exclusive distribution on TikTok and PineDrama, with Hoorae’s shows available for free with ad support.

That backing matters for filmmakers wondering whether they could follow suit. Hoorae has Rae’s reputation, a talent network, and a platform partner — while uploading your own thriller and waiting for the algorithm to fall in love is a different proposition. Still, for this pioneering and hopeful group the relationship has already supported an expanding slate. Following “Screen Time” came “The Compatibility Experiment,” about a couple testing their relationship on a reality dating show, and “Parental Advisory,” which brings affairs, rivalries, and potential murder to the PTA.

“We didn’t want to just try to do exactly what everyone else was doing or what other people were projecting would work,” Clark said. With 10 more microdramas in the works for next year, there should be plenty of secrets to go around. But who pays to keep the confessions coming?

There is serious money in microdramas, although it often comes from asking viewers to pay for the next revelation. Omdia forecasts $1.5 billion in U.S. microdrama revenue in 2026, while its earlier global research found more than 60 percent of revenue came from subscriptions or transactional payments. Hoorae’s approach requires a different calculation, and asked what 580 million views had done for Hoorae financially, Yador described developing relationships instead of revenue.

“It’s important to us that the brands feel integrated into the content rather than it just being slapped on and then you just call it branded content,” Yador said, adding that Hoorae’s in-house sales team seeks brands willing to protect the creative, getting specific about who should hold a product and why. “We’re quite intentional about how we’re engaging with brands that way. And so I think to the consumer lens of it, I think it feels natural and tasteful rather than on the nose branded content.”

Clark said digital production also allows closer collaboration with advertisers than film and television projects involving more partners. “It’s actually been pretty fun building story and these relationships at the same time in a way that also is constantly feeding the financial model in a way that can make sense,” she said. How consistent that model really remains unclear, but Hoorae is enthusiastic.

“This is a volume game,” Yador said. “’How much can you make in X amount of time with X budget?’ — is always a math equation that we’re trying to solve for that feels very one-to-one with just kind of vertical universally. For an industry still contending with declining production in Los Angeles, the prospect of more work is welcome. And what that work pays for matters just as much.

“Screen Time” is a SAG production, with The Wrap reporting on a Verticals Agreement that establishes minimum pay, overtime, and pension and health contributions for Hoorae workerks. Covered productions remain a fraction of the market. And still, Clark and Yador sounded excited to be making things and building profitable artistic environments. As creators, the obstacles were familiar even when the delivery system wasn’t: Find the fans. Make it work. Have we tried a… kiss?

“When we’re on set, we’ve scripted things that this needs to hit, this will drive engagement and it’s not popping,” Clark said, laughing. “So, we’re like, okay, well maybe they need to kiss! Maybe we need a slap! Maybe we need something else here. We’re able to try things in the moment.”

The hope is that those bursts of experimentation can keep adding up to lasting employment at Hoorae. Considering what wanted for the brand’s future, Clark returned to the work: “More TV, more film, more verticals, more people being able to get back to work and sustain themselves on this art.”
